items.readable_text:
Content:
Given a continuous function [MATH: f(x)] on a closed interval [MATH: [a, b],] the mean value theorem for integrals guarantees that there exists a number [MATH: c \in [a,b]] such that

Content:
[MATH: \int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a),]

Content:
which can be visualized as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ebcdedffd8ccc6ebfb935175143a6af5]

Content:
We have a similar theorem for functions with two variables. The so-called mean value theorem for double integrals states:

Content:
> If the function [MATH: f(x,y)] is continuous on a closed and bounded region [MATH: D,] then there exists a point [MATH: (a,b) \in D] such that
> [MATH: \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).]

Content:
This has a nice geometrical interpretation when [MATH: f] is non-negative on [MATH: D.] In this case, the theorem tells us that there exists a point [MATH: (a,b) \in D] such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface [MATH: z=f(x,y)] and the [MATH: xy]-plane over the region [MATH: D] equals the volume of the right cylinder with base [MATH: D] and height [MATH: f(a,b).]

Content:
The diagram below shows the case when [MATH: D] is rectangular, and the corresponding cylinder is a rectangular solid.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/08704028c95e5063ae49094eda8e5410]

Content:
In general, the point [MATH: (a,b)] mentioned in the theorem is not unique. Let's see an example.

items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the continuous function

Content:
[MATH: f(x,y) = x+3y^2+2]

Content:
and the region [MATH: D] given by

Content:
[MATH: D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.]

Content:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point [MATH: (a,b) \in D] such that

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).]

Content:
Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

Content:
[MATH: ∬_(D)f(x, y)dA|= ∬_(D)(x + 3y^{2} + 2)dA; = ∫_{0}^{2}∫_{0}^{2}(x + 3y^{2} + 2)dydx; = ∫_{0}^{2}[xy + y^{3} + 2y]_{y = 0}^{y = 2}dx; = ∫_{0}^{2}(2x + 12)dx; = [x^{2} + 12x]_{x = 0}^{x = 2}; = 28.]

Content:
Next, we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Area}(D) = 2 \cdot 2 = 4.]

Content:
So, our mean-value equation simplifies to

Content:
[MATH: 28|= f(a, b) ⋅ 4; 7|= f(a, b); 7|= a + 3b^{2} + 2; a|= 5 − 3b^{2}.]

Content:
This equation describes part of a parabola in the [MATH: xy]-plane, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/08fb2306a89f9e36c5b5d5d66b6a5bf7]

Content:
To find a particular point that satisfies the mean value theorem, we can set, for example, [MATH: b=1 \in [0,2]] and obtain [MATH: a=2.] So, the point [MATH: (2,1)] satisfies the mean value theorem for double integrals. Consequently, the two solids below must have the same volume.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6bbee10c675a4e2b3b4ac5fc2fb4a4da]

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the function [MATH: f(x,y)] and the region [MATH: D] given by

[MATH: f(x,y) =\dfrac{xy}2, \qquad D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2y, \: 0 \leq y \leq 4 \big\}.]

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point [MATH: (a,b) \in D] such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface [MATH: z=f(x,y)] and the [MATH: xy]-plane over the region [MATH: D] equals the volume of the right cylinder with base [MATH: D] and height [MATH: f(a,b).] Find [MATH: a] given that [MATH: b=2.]
sections.readable_text:
Consider the function [MATH: f(x,y)] and the region [MATH: D] given by

[MATH: f(x,y) =\dfrac{xy}2, \qquad
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2y, \: 0 \leq y \leq 4 \big\}.]

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point [MATH: (a,b) \in D] such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface [MATH: z=f(x,y)] and the [MATH: xy]-plane over the region [MATH: D] equals the volume of the right cylinder with base [MATH: D] and height [MATH: f(a,b).] Find [MATH: a] given that [MATH: b=2.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point [MATH: (a,b) \in D] such that

[MATH: \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).]

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

[MATH: ∬_(D)f(x, y)dA|= ∬_(D)(xy)/(2)dA; = ∫_{0}^{4}∫_{0}^{2y}(xy)/(2)dxdy; = ∫_{0}^{4}[(x^{2}y)/(4)]_{x = 0}^{x = 2y}dy; = ∫_{0}^{4}y^{3}dy; = [(y^{4})/(4)]_{y = 0}^{y = 4}; = 64.]

Next, we have

[MATH: Area(D)|= ∬_(D)dA; = ∫_{0}^{4}∫_{0}^{2y}dxdy; = ∫_{0}^{4}[x]_{x = 0}^{x = 2y}dy; = ∫_{0}^{4}2ydy; = [y^{2}]_{y = 0}^{y = 4}; = 16.]

Also, we are told that [MATH: b=2.] So, our initial equation simplifies to

[MATH: 64|= f(a, 2) ⋅ 16; 64|= (a ⋅ 2)/(2) ⋅ 16; 64|= 16a; a|= 4.]

Notice that [MATH: \left( 4,2 \right) \in D.] Therefore, the answer is [MATH: a = 4.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's sketch our region [MATH: D\mathbin{:}]

Notice that

[MATH: \textrm{Area}(D) = \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot \pi \cdot 1^2 = \dfrac\pi 4.]

The average value of the function over a region [MATH: D] is given by

[MATH: f_{\textrm{ave}} = \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A.]

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

[MATH: \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \: r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.]

In polar coordinates [MATH: (r, \theta),] the region can be expressed as

[MATH: \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq 2\pi\right\}.]

Using the change of variables formula, we obtain

[MATH: ∬_(D)15xy^{2}dA|= ∬_(Δ)15r\cos θ ⋅ (r\sin θ)^{2}rdrdθ; = ∫_{3π/2}^{2π}∫_{0}^{1}15r^{4}\cos θ\sin^{2} θdrdθ; = ∫_{3π/2}^{2π}3\cos θ\sin^{2} θ∫_{0}^{1}5r^{4}drdθ; = ∫_{3π/2}^{2π}3\cos θ\sin^{2} θ[r^{5}]_{0}^{1}dθ; = ∫_{3π/2}^{2π}3\cos θ\sin^{2} θ(1^{5} − 0)dθ; = ∫_{3π/2}^{2π}3\cos θ\sin^{2} θdθ; = [\sin^{3} θ]_{3π/2}^{2π}; = (\sin^{3} (2π) − \sin^{3} ((3π)/(2))); = (0 − (− 1)); = 1.] Therefore,

[MATH: f_{\textrm{ave}} = \dfrac{4}{\pi} \cdot 1 = \dfrac{4}{\pi}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Given a continuous function [MATH: f(x)] on a closed interval [MATH: [a, b],] the mean value theorem for integrals guarantees that there exists a number [MATH: c \in [a,b]] such that

Content:
[MATH: \int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a),]

Content:
which can be visualized as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ebcdedffd8ccc6ebfb935175143a6af5]

Content:
We have a similar theorem for functions with two variables. The so-called mean value theorem for double integrals states:

Content:
> If the function [MATH: f(x,y)] is continuous on a closed and bounded region [MATH: D,] then there exists a point [MATH: (a,b) \in D] such that
> [MATH: \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).]

Content:
This has a nice geometrical interpretation when [MATH: f] is non-negative on [MATH: D.] In this case, the theorem tells us that there exists a point [MATH: (a,b) \in D] such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface [MATH: z=f(x,y)] and the [MATH: xy]-plane over the region [MATH: D] equals the volume of the right cylinder with base [MATH: D] and height [MATH: f(a,b).]

Content:
The diagram below shows the case when [MATH: D] is rectangular, and the corresponding cylinder is a rectangular solid.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/08704028c95e5063ae49094eda8e5410]

Content:
In general, the point [MATH: (a,b)] mentioned in the theorem is not unique. Let's see an example.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Worked Example

Content:
Consider the continuous function

Content:
[MATH: f(x,y) = x+3y^2+2]

Content:
and the region [MATH: D] given by

Content:
[MATH: D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.]

Content:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point [MATH: (a,b) \in D] such that

Content:
[MATH: \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).]

Content:
Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

Content:
[MATH: ∬_(D)f(x, y)dA|= ∬_(D)(x + 3y^{2} + 2)dA; = ∫_{0}^{2}∫_{0}^{2}(x + 3y^{2} + 2)dydx; = ∫_{0}^{2}[xy + y^{3} + 2y]_{y = 0}^{y = 2}dx; = ∫_{0}^{2}(2x + 12)dx; = [x^{2} + 12x]_{x = 0}^{x = 2}; = 28.]

Content:
Next, we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Area}(D) = 2 \cdot 2 = 4.]

Content:
So, our mean-value equation simplifies to

Content:
[MATH: 28|= f(a, b) ⋅ 4; 7|= f(a, b); 7|= a + 3b^{2} + 2; a|= 5 − 3b^{2}.]

Content:
This equation describes part of a parabola in the [MATH: xy]-plane, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/08fb2306a89f9e36c5b5d5d66b6a5bf7]

Content:
To find a particular point that satisfies the mean value theorem, we can set, for example, [MATH: b=1 \in [0,2]] and obtain [MATH: a=2.] So, the point [MATH: (2,1)] satisfies the mean value theorem for double integrals. Consequently, the two solids below must have the same volume.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6bbee10c675a4e2b3b4ac5fc2fb4a4da]

---

Item 3 — Example: Finding Points That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem

Example Prompt:
Consider the function [MATH: f(x,y)] and the region [MATH: D] given by

[MATH: f(x,y) =\dfrac{xy}2, \qquad
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2y, \: 0 \leq y \leq 4 \big\}.]

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point [MATH: (a,b) \in D] such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface [MATH: z=f(x,y)] and the [MATH: xy]-plane over the region [MATH: D] equals the volume of the right cylinder with base [MATH: D] and height [MATH: f(a,b).] Find [MATH: a] given that [MATH: b=2.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point [MATH: (a,b) \in D] such that

[MATH: \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).]

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

[MATH: ∬_(D)f(x, y)dA|= ∬_(D)(xy)/(2)dA; = ∫_{0}^{4}∫_{0}^{2y}(xy)/(2)dxdy; = ∫_{0}^{4}[(x^{2}y)/(4)]_{x = 0}^{x = 2y}dy; = ∫_{0}^{4}y^{3}dy; = [(y^{4})/(4)]_{y = 0}^{y = 4}; = 64.]

Next, we have

[MATH: Area(D)|= ∬_(D)dA; = ∫_{0}^{4}∫_{0}^{2y}dxdy; = ∫_{0}^{4}[x]_{x = 0}^{x = 2y}dy; = ∫_{0}^{4}2ydy; = [y^{2}]_{y = 0}^{y = 4}; = 16.]

Also, we are told that [MATH: b=2.] So, our initial equation simplifies to

[MATH: 64|= f(a, 2) ⋅ 16; 64|= (a ⋅ 2)/(2) ⋅ 16; 64|= 16a; a|= 4.]

Notice that [MATH: \left( 4,2 \right) \in D.] Therefore, the answer is [MATH: a = 4.]

---

Item 4 — Question 1

[MATH: f(x, y) = x^{2} + 2y + 1, D = {(x, y): 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, 0 ≤ y ≤ 3}.]

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point [MATH: (a, b) ∈ D] such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface [MATH: z = f(x, y)] and the [MATH: xy]-plane over the region [MATH: D] equals the volume of the right cylinder with base [MATH: D] and height [MATH: f(a, b).] Find [MATH: b] given that [MATH: a = 1.]

Item 6 — Tutorial: The Average Value of a Function

Content:
Recall that the average value of a continuous function [MATH: f(x)] on a closed interval [MATH: D = [a,b]] is given by

Content:
[MATH: f_\textrm{ave} = \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Length}(D)}\int_a^b f(x) \: \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
There is an analogous definition for functions of two variables, stated below:

Content:
> Suppose [MATH: D] is a closed and bounded region in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] which has non-zero finite area [MATH: \textrm{Area}(D).] If [MATH: f (x, y)] is a continuous function on [MATH: D,] then the average value of [MATH: \boldsymbol f] on [MATH: \boldsymbol D] is given by
> [MATH: f_{\textrm{ave}} =\dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A.]

---

Item 7 — Example: Finding the Average Value of a Function

Example Prompt:
Find the average value of the function [MATH: f(x,y) = xy] on the region [MATH: D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: -1 \leq x \leq 2, \: x \leq y \leq 3x \big\}] given that the area of the region is [MATH: 3] square units.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Applying the average value formula, we find that the average value of the function is

[MATH: f_{ave}|= (1)/(Area(D))∬_(D)f(x, y)dA; = (1)/(3)∬_(D)xydA; = (1)/(3)∫_{− 1}^{2}∫_{x}^{3x}xydydx; = (1)/(3)∫_{− 1}^{2}[(xy^{2})/(2)]_{y = x}^{y = 3x}dx; = (1)/(3)∫_{− 1}^{2}4x^{3}dx; = (1)/(3)[x^{4}]_{x = − 1}^{x = 2}; = (1)/(3)(16 − 1); = 5.]

---
